## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both want to see missed bookings on their own phones before paying, which is one plain group I'd recognise, while Andreas (already has his number and finds the licence too dear for it) and Hannes (won't take a robot at any price) rightly stand apart since neither fits that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all four speak to what the tool is worth.

founder.order_why: Mostly logical, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I already named my first step, the €3,000 pilot at one hotel (20-21), so it reads as an afterthought instead of part of how it sells.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and question; screen 22 (offer a pilot) re-asks what screen 20 already captured as the commitment step.
founder.missing: No place to say the pilot is money-back and credited against the roll-out, or that the €3,000 pilot is followed by a per-hotel monthly licence. Those are the two terms that make the price land with a revenue director.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It went from how many calls we lose, to what it is worth, to budget, sign-off, data protection and then the pilot, and the 'one more thing' follow-up on the 4 weeks to 3 months sat right after the answer it was about.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 partly overlap: 6 asks how long the data protection review would take, and 7 asks what would take the time, where the data protection review is the obvious answer again.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How we cover missed and after-hours calls today, such as a call center, overflow or voicemail, and what that costs us. What a missed call is worth in average booking value. Whether it connects to our PMS/CRS and handles German-speaking guests well.

screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to the owner, to several people, to not my call, and I can't say covers the rest without overlap.
screens.why5: The owner is a role I recognise in a hotel group, and nothing of the product or the founder's own terms reaches me beyond the price I already gave.
screens.why6: One short either-or question, four short options read as a list and one escape at the end, all easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: There is one measure (who has to agree), the fixed four come in order with the founder's role named second, two count for and two against, and I can't say sits apart as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, asking how long the data protection side would hold things up is the obvious next step in buying it.
screens.why2: A Datenschutzprüfung of anything that touches guest calls is everyday language in a German hotel group, and the bands are plain time spans.
screens.why3: I have taken call recording and PMS tools past our Datenschutzbeauftragter before, so I know roughly how long that review takes for us.
screens.why4: The bands run without gaps or overlaps from under 2 weeks to over 6 months, 'It wouldn't be needed' covers a group that already has the calls covered, and 'I can't tell' fits as the only escape.
screens.why5: Only the name Codyco from the idea card appears, the step is a real brake on my side, and nothing of the founder's pitch or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Spoken as four options and then the two bands on the chosen side, I can hold it after one hearing; '2 to under 4 weeks' is slightly clumsy but says fine.
screens.why7: Every option measures how long the review itself would take, the band edge sits at what looks like the founder's 4 weeks (1 month replaced by 4 weeks, the band below reading 'to under'), and two bands plus 'not needed' count for while three count against, so the belief can be supported or refuted, with 'I can't tell' as the one escape.

screens.why1: I just told them the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months, so asking what eats that time follows naturally.
screens.why2: It reads my band back the way I would say it, and Codyco is the name from the idea card, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know what holds this up: the Datenschutzbeauftragter, the works council because guest calls are recorded, the AV contract with the vendor, and the owners' sign-off.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Codyco and the review were shown to me on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences with one question and no symbols or lists, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said 4 weeks to 3 months. What would take the time in the data protection review of guest calls?

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I would actually put money on a pilot at one of our hotels is the natural last question of the buying section.
screens.why2: A paid pilot at one hotel with money back if it does not work is how vendors pitch to us all the time, and €3,000 is a figure I can weigh straight away.
screens.why3: Pilots at one property are my call, inside my sign-off limit, so I answer from what I actually do with vendors.
screens.why4: A firm yes, a yes that wants to see the demo working first, probably not and no cover how I would really respond, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: Codyco and the pilot appear here on purpose under the idea card, and nothing reads like the founder's internal jargon; it is just a priced, money-back trial at one hotel.
screens.why6: One question with four options, the euro amount says well as three thousand euros, and the long first option only repeats the stem, so it is easy to hold.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's step in full, the soft yes is a free smaller step to the same step, two answers are for and two against, there is no escape and No is the floor, so the belief can hold or fail.
